script: Boss chastised me for a late lunch during a "mission critical outage", so I clocked out when the whole network went down!. I was the first IT person the company ever hired. The owner thought I'd be a jack‑of‑all‑trades, the one to fix anything, and that's exactly what I was. But here's the thing… I had no formal training, just a stack of blue‑collar jobs behind me and a laptop that could reboot a factory line. Three days earlier, I was staring at the only computer that ran the shipping software for a hundred packages in the queue. The owner wanted me to keep Windows in place and reinstall programs piece‑by‑piece, because he'd paid extra for tech support. I answered the phone for hours, didn't leave my desk, and when the job finally finished I took a lunch half an hour late. What I didn't know was that the boss was already fuming about lunch breaks. The boss had a strict 12‑1 lunch window policy. I told him I'd come back in a moment, and he slammed the door. I kept my cool because I knew the stakes—if I missed a lunch break, I'd get a ticket, and if I got a ticket, the boss would probably let me down at the next outage. But here's the thing… I was still on my lunch break when the network went down at 12:25. All of the factory's Ethernet cables were unshielded, the machines were humming, and nothing pinged. I had no admin access to the switches or routers because we were subletting the office space. I set up Wireshark to record traffic and ran a continuous ping from my command line, then grabbed a sandwich. The network outage felt like a punch in the gut, and I was stuck outside the office with a sandwich in one hand and a log file in the other. And that's when everything changed… the boss was standing at my desk when I returned. He casually mentioned, "the network is up, by the way!" as if that was the end of it, and then walked away. I had the "I told you so" ready, but I also knew that I was the only one who could see the packet loss. The stakes were real—if I didn't act, the whole day could stall, and I'd be the one blamed. But here's the thing… I'd already made my move, recorded the evidence, and still kept my composure. Later, I sent the Wireshark capture to the owner and explained that the unshielded cables and high‑voltage machines were likely causing the intermittent outages. He thanked me, promised to invest in proper cabling, and, for once, didn't call me out for lunch. I realized the boss was just scared of being the weak link, not that I was. And that's when everything changed—my reputation was solidified, and the owner finally trusted me to make decisions on the fly. The day ended with the network stable, the shipment moving, and me sitting back on my chair, knowing that I'd kept my cool and proved my worth. I closed my laptop, put my badge on, and walked out with a sandwich in one hand and the satisfaction of a job well done. The last thing I said to myself was, "That's the tea for today." And that's the end of the story.
